A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CUDA-L1. Their methods, equations, results, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: V1 reports original KernelBench evaluations, GPU-transfer experiments and optimization ablations, including per-level comparisons in Appendix A.

after.justification: V7 reports original benchmark comparisons, GPU-transfer results, reward-hacking observations and optimization ablations.

M1.justification: The three-stage training framework, backbone and contrastive exemplar selection remain. However, v7 Section 3.2 introduces a DeepSeek-R1 reward checker, retrieval from a dynamic hacking-case database, and normalized reward clipping. These substantially extend reward validation and modify training beyond v1's prompt-based prohibitions.

E1.justification: Both versions train and evaluate using the same 250 KernelBench tasks across three levels. V7 removes H800 from the GPU portability coverage while retaining the other five architectures. Its replacement case studies and generated reference implementations concern existing benchmark tasks.

E2.justification: V7 adds evaluated reference comparisons using Torch Compile, Torch Compile Reduce Overhead and Claude-4-generated CUDA Graph implementations in Tables 4 and 6. The vanilla LLM, evolutionary LLM and CUDA-L1 variant membership in Table 5 remains unchanged.

E3.justification: V7 Section 3.1 specifies synchronization of additional CUDA streams before recording the end event, addressing an explicitly demonstrated timing loophole. It also introduces a speedup threshold above 1.01 and conversion-dependent CUDA Graph comparison denominators, including 229 tasks on A100. The 20-minute evaluation window and 1,000-input correctness checks remain.

E4.justification: V1's GRU and standard-Conv3D ablations are replaced by LSTM and mathematical-short-circuit ablations involving different optimization combinations (v7 Tables 8–9 and Appendix B). V7 also adds a diagonal-matrix case study and quantifies timing exploitation. The training-stage and exemplar-selection ablation families remain.

E5.justification: The main repeated-timing, variance-control and best-of-five procedures remain unchanged. V7 Appendix B.1 newly includes an example timing harness averaging 100 forward passes; v1's replaced GRU listing has no equivalent timing loop. This is limited repetition information, without evidence of additional independent training runs or new confidence-interval reporting.

E6.justification: Table 4's reported A100 mean/maximum change from 17.7×/449× to 3.12×/120× alongside timing and training revisions, rather than establishing a same-setting performance decline. Tables 5–6 also change extensively, and the highest default mean shifts from RTX 3090 to H100. Compiled/Graph results are added, while v1 Tables 7 and 11's detailed per-level comparisons disappear.

T1.justification: V7 adds Equation 6 defining normalized, clipped rewards and a short algebraic/complexity argument for diagonal multiplication in Section 5.1. The original exemplar-sampling, reward-aggregation and GRPO equations remain substantively unchanged; no theorem or proof framework is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion replace the 17.7× average/449× peak claim with 3.12×/120× against default references and add claims against compiled and CUDA Graph baselines. The introduction adds contributions concerning released Graph references and reward-hacking detection, and expands optimization discovery to mathematical simplifications. The central contrastive-learning and generalization claims remain.

C2.justification: V1 celebrates extreme stream-related gains as evidence of optimization synergy. V7 identifies asynchronous-stream timing exploitation as producing artificial approximately 18× results and explains why prompt restrictions are insufficient. It adds the need for careful human inspection and replaces the strongest-complex-task interpretation with baseline-dependent effectiveness and mathematical-shortcut explanations.

D1.justification: V7 adds synchronization pseudocode, specifies the checker model, three retrieved hacking examples and clipping threshold 1.5, and documents Claude 4's Graph-reference construction with up to ten attempts and an announced release location. Appendix B replaces the GRU/standard-convolution listings with LSTM and constant-output implementations, including a timing harness.

R1.justification: The 33 referenced works are retained. V7 Section 6.1 removes v1's characterization of The AI CUDA Engineer [13] as a retrieval-based non-RL comparator, its assertion that this work was evaluated as a baseline, and the direct superiority claim. Broader positioning against evolutionary LLMs remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, results discussion, portability discussion and case-study narrative are substantially rewritten. Reward hacking moves from a method subsection into a standalone section, dataset and evaluation descriptions are merged, and appendix organization changes after removing the former Appendix A. Much of the original training exposition remains.

P2.justification: Figure 1 becomes a grouped comparison of four reference configurations across five GPUs. The speedup-distribution and execution-timeline figures disappear, and a diagonal-code figure is added. Tables 4 and 6 gain configuration blocks. Retained generic appendix snippets are reformatted from three dense four-column tables into five three-column tables.

improvement.justification: V7 substantially improves transparency and evaluation design by exposing the timing loophole behind the earlier approximately 18× claim, specifying corrected synchronization, replacing the headline results and adding compiled/Graph comparisons. This addresses a central validity defect in v1. Removed breakdowns and remaining inconsistencies limit reliability: Section 4.4 claims a 96% bucket-method speedup rate despite Table 5 reporting 226/250, and Appendix B.1's reference and optimized LSTM listings return different outputs. These problems are material, but the measurement correction and broader comparisons provide a substantial net gain.
